title: Taxila: World Heritage List entry (integrity, authenticity, protection and management)
author: UNESCO World Heritage Centre
topic: Taxila, Bhir Mound, Buddhist monasteries, Gandhara, integrity, threats, vegetation, quarrying, earthquakes, looting, Antiquities Act, Master Plan
excerpt: Taxila, inscribed in 1980 under criteria (iii) and (vi), is a serial site comprising a Mesolithic cave, four early settlement sites, Buddhist monasteries, and a Muslim mosque and madrassa; it reached its apogee between the 1st and 5th centuries. Risks to its integrity include exposure of the archaeological remains to the extremes of a tropical climate, overgrown vegetation, earthquakes, expansion of industrial estates, limestone blasting and quarrying, and looting of Buddhist monastery sites. The complex is described as authentic in its forms and design, materials and substance. It is protected under the Antiquities Act of 1975; since the 2010 constitutional amendment the Punjab and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa provincial governments are responsible for its administration, funding is recognised as inadequate, and needed actions include completing a Master Plan, scientific studies of vegetation control, an impact assessment of industry and quarrying, and anti-looting measures.
source_type: UNESCO World Heritage List entry (web page)

title: Archaeological Ruins at Moenjodaro: World Heritage List entry (integrity, authenticity, protection and management)
author: UNESCO World Heritage Centre
topic: Moenjodaro, Mohenjo-daro, Indus Valley civilization, salt action, saline, water table, mud slurry, mud capping, re-pointing, underpinning, brick conservation
excerpt: Inscribed in 1980, Moenjodaro is described as the best preserved urban settlement in South Asia dating back to the beginning of the 3rd millennium BC, on the right bank of the Indus. Its foundations are threatened by saline action due to a rise of the water table of the Indus River; a 1970s UNESCO campaign partially mitigated damage to the mud-brick buildings, and only about one third of the 240 ha has been excavated since 1922. Salt action, thermal stress and rain are addressed through a holistic approach that includes mud slurry, mud capping, re-pointing and underpinning, supported by a site laboratory using traditional methods. Flood risk has been partly reduced by embankments and spurs. The site is protected under the Antiquities Act of 1975, a Master Plan was prepared by the Department of Archaeology and Museums, and management passed to the Culture Department of Sindh under the 18th Amendment.
source_type: UNESCO World Heritage List entry (web page)

title: Archaeological Ruins at Moenjodaro (Pakistan): State of Conservation, Decision 46 COM 7B.38
author: UNESCO World Heritage Committee
topic: Moenjodaro, salt crystallization, hydration, moisture, erosion, flooding 2022, conservation manual, mud slurry, mud plaster, salt-laden earth, heritage impact assessment, drainage
excerpt: The 2024 decision on the state of conservation of Moenjodaro cites salt crystallization and hydration inside masonry as a main cause of decay. The mission found that intensive saline action and moisture leading to rapid erosion continue because they arise from the property's geological conditions, and that stagnant water weakens wall bases. The Conservation Manual sets out three remedial actions: application of mud slurry, application of mud plaster, and replacement of salt-laden earth. Heritage Impact Assessments must be submitted for review prior to making any irreversible decisions. The site was affected by monsoon rainfall and flooding in August 2022; the Committee commended the State Party's response, asked it to implement the March 2024 mission recommendations, and requested an updated report by 1 December 2025.
source_type: UNESCO World Heritage Committee decision and state of conservation page (web page)

title: Jamalgarhi (Gandhara Connections introductory essay, Version 2)
author: Rienjang, Wannaporn (Gandhara Connections, University of Oxford)
topic: Jamal Garhi, Jamalgarhi, Gandhara, Buddhist monastery, main stupa, circular base, chapels, diaper masonry, rubble masonry, excavation history, sculptures
excerpt: Jamalgarhi is a Buddhist monastery in the Peshawar valley on a hilltop above a village, near Takht-i-Bahi and Sahr-i-Bahlol; coin finds suggest it was in use from about AD 100 to about AD 400. The Main Stupa has a circular base ringed by fifteen chapels, unusual because Gandharan stupas usually have square bases, and is linked by stairs to a series of courtyards containing chapels, small stupas and rooms. Except for the Conference Hall, the buildings use diaper masonry, and some walls use rubble masonry. Cunningham discovered the site in 1848, and major excavations took place in 1873 and in 1920 to 1923. None of the schist sculptures recovered by Cunningham in the Main Stupa area were found in situ, and no comprehensive and systematic record of the sculptural finds was made, which makes tracing individual pieces difficult.
source_type: Scholarly essay (PDF), page numbers as printed in the essay

title: Buddhist Ruins of Takht-i-Bahi and Neighbouring City Remains at Sahr-i-Bahlol: World Heritage List entry
author: UNESCO World Heritage Centre
topic: Takht-i-Bahi, Sahr-i-Bahlol, Gandhara, Buddhist monastery, diaper masonry, lime mortar, vegetation, drainage, encroachment, conservation concerns
excerpt: Inscribed in 1980 under criterion (iv), the property consists of the Takht-i-Bahi monastery, founded in the early 1st century AD and used until the 7th century on hilltops of 36.6 to 152.4 metres, and Sahr-i-Bahlol, a small fortified Kushan-period town about 5 km away. The hilltop location protected Takht-i-Bahi from successive invasions, so it is exceptionally well preserved; its stone construction retains the Gandhara diaper-style materials and techniques. Concerns listed include uncontrolled vegetation as a main cause of decay, inadequate drainage, insufficient security against illegal digging, pollution from factories and traffic, insufficient documentation of the remains, a shortage of craftsmen trained in diaper-pattern techniques, and encroachment at Sahr-i-Bahlol where houses have been built on the ruins. Both components are protected under the Ancient Preservation Act (1904) and the Antiquity Act (1975); a Master Plan was prepared in 2011 and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa declared a 445-hectare Archaeological Reserve.
source_type: UNESCO World Heritage List entry (web page)

title: Fort and Shalamar Gardens in Lahore: World Heritage List entry
author: UNESCO World Heritage Centre
topic: Lahore Fort, Shalamar Gardens, Mughal architecture, Shish Mahal, Sheesh Mahal, hydraulic works, List in Danger, authenticity, management, master plan
excerpt: Inscribed in 1981 under criteria (i), (ii) and (iii), the property comprises two Mughal royal complexes about 7 km apart: the Lahore Fort and the Shalimar Gardens, outstanding examples of Mughal artistic expression of the 16th and 17th centuries; the Shish Mahal (1631-32) is described as one of the most beautiful palaces in the world. The 1999 destruction of two of the Shalimar Gardens' three hydraulic works significantly marred the integrity of the Gardens, and the property was on the List of World Heritage in Danger from 2000 to 2012. Authenticity of layout, form, design and substance is largely retained, but authenticity of function and setting has been eroded over time. The property is protected under the Antiquities Act (1975) and managed by the Directorate General of Archaeology, Punjab, under two Master Plans and five-year preservation programmes launched in 2006-2007; identified threats include deterioration of monuments, urban encroachment and poor coordination among agencies.
source_type: UNESCO World Heritage List entry (web page)

title: Fort and Shalamar Gardens in Lahore: State of Conservation, Decision 23 COM X.B.43
author: UNESCO World Heritage Committee
topic: Lahore Fort, Shalamar Gardens, efflorescence, moisture, peripheral walls, ground level, non-traditional materials, Shish Mahal mirror hall, stucco ceiling, hydraulic works, ICOMOS mission
excerpt: Following an ICOMOS expert mission in October-November 1998, Pakistan adopted 17 recommendations for the property. At Shalamar Gardens the expert reported a general state of disrepair of the structural components and buildings; uneven inner and outer ground levels caused moisture damage and efflorescence on the peripheral walls, and fountain water channels were leaking. At the Lahore Fort, non-traditional building materials had been used in restoration and no overall Management Plan existed; in the Shish Mahal Mirror Hall the convex mirror glass was cracking away from the carved stucco ceiling and structural stability was a concern. The Bureau recommended that Pakistan examine lowering the ground level around the peripheral walls, and the Committee expressed concern over the demolition of the 375-year-old essential hydraulic works of the Shalamar Gardens and requested urgent corrective measures.
source_type: UNESCO World Heritage Committee decision and state of conservation page (web page)
